Sickle Cell Disease
Introduction
Genetic condition inherited in the autosomal recessive form
In the United States, sickle cell disease (SCD) affects approximately 100,000 individuals.1 It
occurs in approximately 1 of every 365 Black or African-American births.

Introduction
SCD is a multisystem disorder, caused by a single gene mutation2 producing an amino
acid substitution in the hemoglobin molecule of sickle cells (HbS), which is a variant of
normal adult hemoglobin.3
SCD denotes all genotypes containing at least one sickle gene, in which HbS makes up at
least one-half the hemoglobin present.3 In addition to the homozygotic HbS disease
(sickle cell anemia), five other major sickle genotypes are linked to the disease, including
variants such as hemoglobin C and beta (ß)-thalassemia (compound heterozygosity).3
Dissimilar from individuals with SCD, individuals with sickle cell trait carry only one
defective gene, and HbS makes up less than 40% of the hemoglobin present.4
Approximately 1 in 13 Black or African-American babies are born with sickle cell trait.
They typically live normal lives.
Pathophysiology

The surface of the variant β-globin (βS globin) chain has an amino acid substitution
(hydrophobic valine for hydrophilic glutamic acid), resulting from a single nucleotide
substitution (GTG for GAG) in the sixth codon of the β-globin gene.5
Changes in the βS globin chain allows HbS to polymerize if deoxygenated. This polymerization
of deoxygenated HbS is the primary event in the molecular pathogenesis of SCD.2,3
After it is polymerized, HbS acquires a rope-like structure that, if aligned with other
polymerized HbS molecules, forms a bundle that distorts the red cell into the classic crescent
or sickled forms.

Pathophysiology
Vaso-occlusive crisis, a staple of SCD, originally was attributed to microcirculatory
obstruction from impaired erythrocyte deformability during capillary transit as a result
of the sickle cell shape. Currently, the process of microcirculatory obstruction appears to
be multifactorial. These factors are prolongation of the erythrocyte microvascular transit
time (secondary to enhanced cell adhesion to endothelium,6-8 abnormal cation
homeostasis with irreversible sickle formation9,10 and abnormal vasomotor tone
favoring vasoconstriction); reduction in time to HbS polymerization, usually caused by
red-cell deoxygenation, an increase in intracellular HbS concentration, and a fall in pH;
and the effect of other tissue modulators (free-radical release and coagulation activation
with pro-adhesive thrombin formation).3
Vaso-occlusion typically causes acute complications, including ischemic damage to
tissues, resulting in severe pain or organ failure.2 In addition to vaso-occlusion,
hemolytic anemia results from the destruction of sickled cells by inflammatory
processes, cell dehydration, and direct membrane damage.11
Diagnosis
Every newborn is screened for SCD via isoelectric focusing, hemoglobin electrophoresis, DNA
analysis, or some combination thereof.5

Because children with SCD have an increased risk of pneumococcal infection and other health
problems, early diagnosis and management are important.
Clinical Manifestations
SCD is a multisystem disorder that may affect the cardiothoracic system (acute chest
syndrome, pulmonary hypertension, chronic restrictive lung disease, left ventricular diastolic
disease, dysrhythmias, sudden death); the nervous system (acute ischemic stroke, proliferative
retinopathy, orbital infarction, silent cerebral infarction, venous sinus thrombosis,
hemorrhagic stroke); the reticuloendothelial system (splenic sequestration, hyposplenism,
anemia, hemolysis); the musculoskeletal system (marrow hyperplasia, osteonecrosis); the
urinary system (papillary necrosis, proteinuria, renal failure, hematuria, priapism); and the
gastrointestinal system (cholelithiasis, cholangiopathy, mesenteric occlusion, and
hepatopathy).2

Clinical Manifestations
In addition to osteonecrosis (most commonly affecting the long bones, ribs, sternum,
spine, and pelvis), the complex cycle of vaso-occlusion and hemolysis may result in other
musculoskeletal complications, including pain crisis and infections.4,12 Multiple factors
can precipitate a vaso-occlusive crisis, including cold weather, hypoxia, infection,
dehydration, stress, and pregnancy.
With microvascular occlusion, inflammatory mediators activate nociceptive afferent
nerve fibers, evoking a pain response.2
Changes in the normal bone microarchitecture are observed as a result of marrow
hyperplasia secondary to chronic hemolysis, with cortical thinning and collapse.13 In
patients with SCD, most of the marrow space tends to be preserved as red marrow,
rather than being converted to normal yellow (fatty) marrow during childhood.14
Compared with unaffected subjects, patients with SCD have lower bone mineral density,
especially in the vertebral region.15 This lower density has been attributed to marrow

hyperplasia.15-18
In the spine, marrow hyperplasia can cause ischemia of the central portion of the
vertebral growth plate, leading to collapse of the vertebrae and a typical H-shape
deformity.14
Impaired growth has been described in patients with SCD, usually as a result of
premature closure of the physis, collapse of the epiphysis because of marrow ischemia,
and impaired growth of the long bones.12,19-21
Participation in sports should be monitored carefully; increased risks of heat illness,
exertional rhabdomyolysis, splenic infarct, and death have been reported.22
Osteonecrosis
In general, vaso-occlusive events may affect the diaphysis and epiphysis, resulting in medullary
infarcts and osteonecrosis, respectively.4
The prevalence of osteonecrosis in patients with SCD is difficult to assess; most studies report
a prevalence of approximately 10%.23,24 MRI studies have found osteonecrosis in the
epiphyses in as many as 41% of adults and 27% of children with SCD.24,25
The most common site of osteonecrosis is the femoral head, followed by the head of the
humerus, the knee, and the small joints of the hands and feet.4,12,14,26,27

Osteonecrosis
Symptomatic patients report painful, limited motion of the affected joint. Plain
radiographs may demonstrate mottled attenuation of the epiphysis, followed by
flattening, sclerosis, and subchondral collapse.13 These changes may be followed by
narrowing of the joint space, joint sclerosis, and osteophyte formation.14

Early disease is best diagnosed via MRI, which shows a high signal intensity on T2-
weighted images in the affected areas outlined by a low-signal–intensity serpiginous
line.4,12 Unmanaged, approximately 87% of affected femoral heads collapse within 5
years of diagnosis.27 Most patients with symptoms of hip osteonecrosis show
progression of collapse, pain, and disability within 3 years of initial presentation; almost
95% will require surgical treatment for intractable pain.27
Osteonecrosis of the hip developing in a young child may result in proximal femur
deformity, including a short femoral neck, a coxa magna and plana, and limb-length
discrepancy.12,28 An elevated hemoglobin-to-hematocrit ratio, a strong predictor for the
presence of osteonecrosis, can be used to determine the need for MRI in asymptomatic
patients.29
Multiple treatment options have been described for symptomatic patients without
evidence of collapse, including autologous bone marrow grafting, core decompression,
osteotomy, and temporary unloading of the affected area4 (Figure 1).

core decompression in patients with SCD. At a mean follow-up of 3 years, the patients
who underwent a combination of surgical treatment and physical therapy did not show
clinical improvement compared with the patients who underwent physical therapy
alone.30-32
Multiple epiphyseal drilling with autologous bone marrow cell implantation enables
short-term improvements in pain and range of motion, with minimal morbidity.33
Osteotomies have been described as salvage procedures in skeletally immature patients
with osteonecrosis.34,35

Total hip arthroplasty in patients with SCD may be challenging, but it appears that the
outcomes in properly selected patients have improved.36-39 A high rate of intraoperative
fractures has been described.39 Cemented components have been associated with
higher revision rates, whereas uncemented components are associated with a higher
risk of intraoperative complications.39
Osteomyelitis
Compared with the general population, patients with SCD are more susceptible to infections,
including osteomyelitis.12 Several mechanisms are postulated for this finding, including
hyposplenism, impaired complement activity, and the presence of infarcted or necrotic
bone.12
Osteomyelitis usually presents with pain, swelling and tenderness, most commonly affecting
the femur, tibia, or humerus.
Fever and elevated inflammatory markers are common.40-42 The clinical presentation of
osteomyelitis is very similar to that of a vaso-occlusive crisis, making the distinction between a
painful crisis and osteomyelitis extremely difficult.4,12

Osteomyelitis
Osteomyelitis may not be suspected until the signs and symptoms of a typical painful
crisis have failed to resolve after 1 to 2 weeks of standard therapy, including intravenous
fluids, oxygenation, and NSAIDs.26 Patients not responding to treatment may need to
undergo advanced imaging. The diagnosis usually is confirmed via positive blood
cultures or bone aspirate obtained from the suspected infection site.43
Salmonella species (as a result of asplenia) and Staphylococcus aureus are the most
common causative organisms associated with osteomyelitis in these populations. The
key to management is early recognition with early antibiotic treatment and, if necessary,
surgical débridement for patients not responding to antibiotic treatment or those with

weeks.4,43
Bone Infarction Versus Osteomyelitis
Differentiation between bone infarction and acute osteomyelitis is a challenge in patients with
SCD.
Bone infarction is 20 to 50 times more common than osteomyelitis in patients with SCD.46,47
It is relatively common to observe mildly elevated inflammatory markers and pain in multiple
anatomic locations in patients with bone infarction; however, the presence of fever is
uncommon. It has been suggested that a longer period of pain and fever higher than 100.8°F
before presentation, and a high C-reactive protein level are predictors of osteomyelitis.42,48

Bone Infarction Versus Osteomyelitis
Plain radiographs usually are not helpful in differentiating these conditions during the
early stages. Although radionuclide bone marrow scanning and bone scanning have
been used to differentiate these two entities, the high radiation dose associated with
nuclear medicine imaging has made these techniques less desirable. The imaging
modality currently preferred for the diagnosis of acute osteomyelitis is gadolinium-
enhanced MRI,49 which is associated with a sensitivity of 92% and a specificity of 96%.50
Contrast material enhancement on MRI in a patient with SCD may enable accurate
distinction between infection and infarction.51 Management of bone infarction generally
is supportive and includes the administration of analgesic agents, hydration, and
antibiotic agents if coexistent infection is suspected.
Septic Arthritis
Septic arthritis occurs in approximately 0.3% of adults and 5% of children with SCD.52
The hip is one of the most common sites of joint infection; positive joint fluid cultures are
observed in more than 95% of patients. S aureus and gram-negative species are the most

Anesthetic and Surgical Risks
Patients with SCD have a high risk of perioperative complications; surgery-related deaths occur
in as many as 7% of this population.53
Multiple risks factors are associated with a postoperative vaso-occlusive crisis, including
decreased oxygen saturation, opioid-induced respiratory depression, fluid shifts, and
variations in body temperature.

Anesthetic and Surgical Risks
Multidisciplinary collaboration and communication between the surgeon,
anesthesiologist, hematologist, and blood bank specialist are key factors in planning for
surgery in this patient population.54
Multiple preventive measures should be adopted to increase the safety of surgical
procedures in patients with SCD, including maintaining appropriate patient hydration
and oxygenation (with anticipation of blood loss and fluid shifts), avoiding acidosis,
maintaining normothermia, and achieving adequate pain control.54
Preoperative transfusions are controversial.54 A conservative preoperative transfusion
regimen to achieve a hemoglobin level of 10 g/dL usually is recommended before major
surgical procedures to prevent perioperative hypoxia.55,56 Smaller procedures, such as
tonsillectomy, ear tube implantation, hernia repair, arthroscopy, and closed reduction,
usually can be performed without preoperative transfusion.4
Acute chest syndrome—an acute pulmonary illness characterized by pulmonary
consolidation and a combination of fever, chest pain, cough, dyspnea, and tachypnea—
accounts for approximately 25% of deaths in patients with SCD.14 Although the illness

Hemophilia
Introduction
Hemophilia is a bleeding disorder inherited as a sex-linked recessive trait.
It is characterized by a deficiency of coagulation factor VIII (hemophilia A) or factor IX
(hemophilia B).
Hemophilia A is estimated to account for 80% to 85% of all hemophilia cases.58
The prevalence of hemophilia A and B has been calculated to be approximately 8.4 and 3.8 for
every 100,000 males, respectively.59,60 Approximately 30% of cases result from spontaneous
genetic variants.
Pathogenesis of Hemophilic Arthropathy
Approximately 80% of all acute bleeds occurring in patients with hemophilia are located in the
musculoskeletal system, including the joints (most commonly the ankle, knee, and elbow
joints) and muscles (iliopsoas and gastrocnemius).61,62
Recurrent joints bleeds may lead to severe joint damage and major morbidity. The synovial
membrane typically is well vascularized. Therefore, synovial joints are susceptible to
spontaneous bleeds.

Pathogenesis of Hemophilic Arthropathy
Recurrent joint bleeding leads to hemophilic arthropathy, a process characterized by
synovial inflammation, cartilage degeneration, and bone resorption.63,64 Synovial
inflammation leads to synovial hypertrophy and vascular remodeling. The inflamed
synovium produces proinflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin-1, interleukin-6 and
tumor necrosis factor-alpha, and plasmin and matrix metalloproteinases that directly
induce cartilage degeneration.65 The presence of blood inside the joint also has a direct
deleterious effect on cartilage. Chondrocytes exposed to proinflammatory cytokines

(derived from blood and the synovial membrane) produce hydrogen peroxide.65 In the
presence of erythrocyte-derived iron, hydrogen peroxide reacts to generate toxic
hydroxyl radicals, which are responsible for chondrocyte apoptosis.65 Inflammation
activates the receptor activator of nuclear factor-kappa B ligand-receptor activator of
nuclear factor-kappa B/osteoprotegerin pathway, resulting in bone resorption by
osteoclasts. As hemophilic arthropathy progresses, an imbalance between osteoclastic
bone resorption and osteoblastic bone formation alters bone remodeling.66
Clinical Presentation
Easy bruising; spontaneous bleeding into the joints, muscles, or soft tissues; or excessive
bleeding after trauma or surgery
Newborns and children younger than 2 years with severe hemophilia commonly present with
soft-tissue and intramuscular bleeding, bleeding associated with medical procedures, and
mucocutaneous bleeding.67,68
A detailed bleeding history and family history of unexplained bleeding in siblings or maternal
male relatives should be obtained if hemophilia is suspected.
Definitive diagnosis is based on a factor VIII or factor IX assay demonstrating deficiency.

Clinical Presentation
The severity of bleeding manifestations in patients with hemophilia is correlated with the
degree of clotting factor deficiency. If clotting factor levels are less than 1% of normal,
the bleeding deficiency is considered severe; levels between 1% and 5% of normal are
considered moderate; and levels between 5% and 40% of normal are considered mild.
Patients with severe hemophilia typically present with spontaneous bleeding into joints
and muscles. Patients with moderate hemophilia have occasional spontaneous bleeding
and prolonged bleeding with minor trauma or surgery. Those with mild hemophilia have
severe bleeding with major trauma or surgery (Figure 2).

General Principles of Management
The Role of Prophylaxis
Prophylaxis for patients with hemophilia consists of the regular administration of clotting
factors, with the aim of maintaining hemostasis to prevent bleeding.
Avoiding joint bleeds is critical in minimizing the risk of arthropathy and disability.

The Role of Prophylaxis
In contrast to episodic replacement therapy (also known as on-demand therapy), in
which clotting factors are administered only at the time of a bleed, prophylaxis can
change the natural history of hemophilia by preventing joint bleeding and maintaining
healthy joints. Therefore, prophylaxis always is recommended over episodic therapy.
Innovative nonfactor replacement therapies that can be administered subcutaneously,
intravenously, or otherwise are being increasingly used for the regular administration of

a hemostatic agent or agents designed to enhance hemostasis and effectively prevent
bleeding in patients with hemophilia69-71
To prevent spontaneous and breakthrough hemarthrosis that may lead to joint disease,
the World Federation of Hemophilia recommends early initiation of prophylaxis with
clotting factor concentrates for pediatric patients with severe hemophilia A or B before
the onset of joint disease and ideally before age 3years.58 Adolescent and adult patients
with hemophilia who have not been treated via prophylaxis and in whom evidence of
joint damage is present should receive tertiary prophylaxis to reduce the number of
hemarthrosis episodes and slow down the progression of hemophilic arthropathy.58
Comprehensive Care
A multidisciplinary team typically is necessary for the diagnosis and management of
hemophilia and its complications.
The goal of comprehensive care is to promote the physical health and psychosocial well-being
of patients affected by hemophilia, ultimately improving their quality of life and reducing their
morbidity and mortality.72,73

Comprehensive Care
Comprehensive care requires more than management of acute bleeding episodes. It also
focuses on the prevention of bleeding and joint damage, the prompt management and
rehabilitation of bleeds, pain management, the management of musculoskeletal
complications including arthropathy, the management of comorbidities, dental care,
psychosocial support, and genetic counselling.58
Hemostatic Agents
Immediate access to clotting factors and/or other hemostatic agents is of key importance for
patients with hemophilia.

In general, the availability of such products for home therapy enables optimal early treatment,
resulting in less pain, dysfunction, and long-term disability, as well as greatly reduced
hospitalization rates.74,75

Hemostatic Agents
Home therapy should be initiated only after the patient has been evaluated by a
comprehensive care team and has received proper education and training in recognizing
bleeds and common complications, dosage calculation, aseptic techniques,
venipuncture, and self-infusion. Close supervision by a comprehensive care team is
required.75,76
Different types of hemostatic agents and coagulation therapies are available for the
treatment of patients with hemophilia. In general, clotting factor concentrates are the
preferred treatment option because they are safe and effective in preventing and
managing bleeds. Clotting factor concentrates can be divided into two main types: virally
inactivated plasma-derived products and genetically engineered recombinant products.
In the presence of factor VIII or factor IX alloantibodies (called inhibitors), bypassing
agents that circumvent the need for factor VIII or factor IX replacement are used for the
management and prevention of bleeding complications.69 Other agents also can be
helpful in the treatment of patients with hemophilia, including desmopressin,
tranexamic acid, and epsilon aminocaproic acid. Recently, nonfactor replacement
therapies with alternative modes of delivery (eg, subcutaneous), a longer half-life, lower
or no risk of inhibitor formation, and a very low burden of administration (eg, up to
monthly dosing), have become available.77

limitations in joint range of motion (Figure 3)


Joint Bleeding
In patients with an acute hemarthrosis, the treatment goal should be to stop the
bleeding as soon as possible before the onset of overt swelling, loss of joint function,
and pain.78 Administration of clotting factor concentrate should begin immediately after
the appearance of a joint bleed.79 In addition to clinical examination, ultrasonography
aids in the identification of acute bleeds.80 An excellent response to management is
defined as a complete resolution of signs and symptoms of bleeding within 8 hours of
the initial infusion of clotting factor concentrate and no additional need for clotting
factor replacement within 72 hours after the onset the of bleeding.58
Acute hemarthrosis episodes usually are painful. Effective pain management usually
includes the prompt administration of clotting factor replacement and effective
analgesia.
Joint aspiration should be considered in patients experiencing a tense, painful
hemarthrosis that shows no improvement within 24 hours of the initial infusion of

clotting factor or if clinical suspicion of infection or septic arthritis exists.79,81,82 If
undergoing joint aspiration, patients should receive clotting factor replacement. After
aspiration, the joint should be immobilized with mild compression.
Synovitis
After acute hemarthrosis, the synovium becomes inflamed, highly vascular, and friable.
Symptoms may take several weeks to resolve.62,83,84
If not properly managed, recurrent hemarthroses and subclinical bleeds ensue.61,62
Regular clinical evaluations are necessary to ensure that the joint returns to a normal stage,
has no evidence of residual effusion or synovitis, and has full functional recovery.85
Nonsurgical and surgical treatment options have been described for the management of
chronic synovitis.

Synovitis
If bleeding persists, the synovium does not return to its original state; it becomes
chronically inflamed and hypertrophic, and the joint becomes prone to additional
bleeding. A vicious cycle of bleeding, loss of joint motion, and inflammation is
established.83 If this process exceeds 3 months, it is defined as chronic synovitis. Over
time, this process leads to irreversible cartilage and bone damage.83,86
In managing chronic synovitis, the aim is to reduce the activity and inflammation of the
synovial membrane.81,87 Nonsurgical treatment options include short-term
administration of clotting factor prophylaxis (in patients not on regular prophylaxis),
physical therapy, and the use of selective cyclooxygenase-2 inhibitors.88,89
For patients in a stage of chronic synovitis with persistent bleeding no longer responding
to nonsurgical treatment options, ablation of the synovial membrane via nonsurgical
synoviorthesis or surgical open or arthroscopic synovectomy is indicated.90-92

Nonsurgical radioisotopic or chemical synovectomy usually is considered the first
treatment option.58 In general, radioisotopic synovectomy (or radiosynovectomy) is
indicated for synovitis causing two or more bleeds in a particular joint for more than 6
months, despite adequate coverage with clotting factor replacement.85
Radiosynovectomy using a pure beta emitter is a simple outpatient procedure, highly
effective in reducing bleeding, and associated with few adverse effects.90,93-100 Clotting
factor prophylaxis should be administered before radiosynovectomy. The simultaneous
administration of intra-articular steroids also is recommended.58 After injection, the joint
should be immobilized for 24 to 48 hours. Then, rehabilitation to regain strength,
proprioception, and function of the joint should begin,101,102 Chemical synovectomy,
using rifampicin or oxytetracycline chlorhydrate, usually is considered if the availability
of radioisotopes is limited.103-105 Chemical synovectomy usually requires multiple
injections and typically is painful. Its administration should be combined with an intra-
articular local anesthetic and an oral analgesic.103-105
Selective embolization of vessels supplying the synovial member of the involved joint has
been described for patients in whom chronic synovitis is resistant to management via
radiosynovectomy.106
If less invasive and equally effective alternatives fail to control chronic synovitis, surgical
synovectomy should be considered. Arthroscopic and open techniques have been
described.107,108 Arthroscopic synovectomy usually is preferred over open synovectomy
because functional recovery usually is better.109 Surgical synovectomy often is indicated
as an additional procedure in patients undergoing surgical treatment or patients with
advanced hemophilic arthropathy.110,111
Advanced Hemophilic Arthropathy
Usually results from a progressive process evolving from hemarthrosis and leading to acute
synovitis, chronic synovitis, and joint degeneration
Often manifests during the teenage years, especially if the patient has had limited or no access
to prophylactic clotting factor therapy

Over time, the synovial membrane and capsule undergo a process of fibrosis, resulting in
additional stiffness.

Advanced Hemophilic Arthropathy
MRI and ultrasonography usually aid in the evaluation of the early stages of arthropathy,
including osteochondral and soft-tissue changes.112-114 Plain radiographs usually are
reserved for the assessment of late arthropathic changes.115-117
The treatment options for chronic hemophilic arthropathy depend on the stage of the
condition, severity of the symptoms, patient age and functional limitations, and available
resources. Specific pain management strategies have been described for patients with
hemophilic arthropathy.58 Physical therapy targeted at preserving muscle strength and
functional ability should be initiated as soon as feasible. Several nonsurgical treatment
techniques have been described for the management of chronic hemophilic arthropathy,
including serial cast immobilization to correct deformities,118,119 traction devices,
bracing and orthotics,120 and walking aids.
If pain relief and functional improvements are not achieved via nonsurgical treatment
measures, surgical treatment options may be necessary. In general, surgical treatment
options include synovectomy and joint débridement,110,121 soft-tissue releases to
manage extra-articular contractures,122 osteotomies to correct angular deformities,123
external fixators to assist in joint deformity correction,124 arthroplasty,125-130 radial
head excision,110,131 and ankle fusion.132
Arthroplasty is indicated in patients with advanced hemophilic arthropathy who have
associated pain and functional limitation that does not respond to nonsurgical
management. A multidisciplinary team that includes experienced orthopaedic surgeons
and hematologists, nurses, social workers, and physical therapists, as well as
appropriate laboratory support are required in considering arthroplasty in this patient
population. For patients undergoing arthroplasty under clotting factor coverage, deep

An injury or sudden stretch may result in a muscle bleed.
Clinically, a muscle bleed is characterized by pain and/or swelling with an associated functional

Early and aggressive management is essential to minimize the risk of permanent contractures,

leg, and anterior compartments of the forearm) may be associated with neurovascular

syndrome secondary to an unmanaged muscle bleed, clotting factor replacement should
be initiated as soon as the patient recognizes the first signs of discomfort or immediately

Pseudotumors
Unmanaged, hemophilic pseudotumors can become very large, compressing
neurovascular structures. Fistulas to the skin are not uncommon. Similar to muscle
bleeds, pseudotumors can be evaluated via ultrasonography, CT, and MRI. The
management of pseudotumors depends on several factors, including location, size,
speed of growth, and effect on adjacent structures. Treatment options include clotting
factor replacement,139,140 aspiration,141,142 embolization,143 radiation,143,144 and
surgical excision.85 If surgical management is performed, the pseudotumor and its
pseudocapsule should be excised, rather than evacuating the hematoma within the
pseudotumor (Figure 5).

Introduction
Gaucher disease is a rare disorder caused by a deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme
glucocerebrosidase. The disease was first described in 1882 by Phillippe Charles Ernest
Gaucher,146 who noted massive splenic enlargement; however, the cause of the disease
was not discovered until 1965 by Brady et al.147 Brady et al147 described the lack of
glucocerebrosidase, causing a toxic buildup of the lipid glucocerebroside in
macrophages and leading to end organ dysfunction.
Epidemiology, Pathogenesis, and Genetics
Gaucher disease is one of the most common lipid lysosomal storage diseases, with a
prevalence of 1 in 40,000 in the general population and 1 in 400 to 600 in the Ashkenazi Jewish
population; however, most affected patients are not Jewish.
Gaucher disease is transmitted via an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Currently,
three types are described.
Type 1 is non-neuronopathic and is the most common form. Patients typically present with
substantial splenomegaly, hematologic disorders, and various orthopaedic
manifestations.148
Type 2 is the acute infantile neuronopathic form. Affected patients usually have considerable
central nervous system involvement, typically leading to death by age 2 or younger.
Type 3 is the subacute/chronic neuronopathic type. It is the least common form and is most
commonly observed in Swedish patients from the county of Norrbotten. The presentation
includes some of the findings observed in patients with type 1, including organomegaly and
hematologic and orthopaedic manifestations, along with less severe forms of the neurologic
findings observed in patients with type 2149-151 (Table 1).

Clinical manifestations arise from accumulated glucocerebroside in macrophages called
Gaucher cells, leading to end organ dysfunction. Symptoms of this dysfunction usually
manifest between 12 and 24 months of age; however, some patients may have no clinical signs
into adulthood.
Splenomegaly is a common presenting symptom, and the spleen may be enlarged to 5 to 75
times normal as the Gaucher cells build up in the spleen152 (Figure 6).

Patients may present with severe pain, fever, leukocytosis, and an elevated erythrocyte
sedimentation rate. Therefore, differentiation from osteomyelitis can be aided by
Technetium-99m bone scintigraphy. A negative study supports the diagnosis of a bone

Osteonecrosis may be intramedullary and subcortical, typically involving the femoral head,
distal femur, tibial plateau and proximal humerus. Osteoarticular collapse from
osteonecrosis may lead to substantial disability and pain.
The osteonecrosis is thought to result from abnormalities in coagulation, leading to
thrombosis. Elevated D-dimer levels also may be observed, supporting this presumed
mechanism.
Despite the pain and subchondral collapse, only 13% of adults in a large series of patients
with Gaucher disease underwent joint arthroplasty.153
Surgical treatment in patients with Gaucher disease is associated with a higher than normal
rate of complications. Along with major risks of bleeding, patients with Gaucher disease
experience poor wound healing and a high risk of gram-positive infection because of
macrophage incompetence.156
Deformity is caused by the suppression of osteoclast activity, leading to poor remodeling in
children and poor fracture healing in all patients. The classic deformity is observed in the
distal femur or proximal tibia and is known as the Erlenmeyer flask appearance, which
typically is asymptomatic. This deformity is observed in 60% to 80% of patients with Gaucher
disease but is not pathognomonic because it also may be observed in patients with other
forms of skeletal dysplasia152 (Figure 7).
Osteopenia is common, and thinning of the cortices is observed in almost every patient with
Gaucher disease. Cortical thinning also may appear as a discrete lytic lesion.157,158
Pathologic fracture and vertebral compression fractures also are common; as many as 23%
of patients experience some form of pathologic fracture.153
The management of fractures may be a challenge because of the poor healing of bone and
the high risk of bleeding and infection with surgical management. Delayed union and
nonunion are common.
Vertebral compression fracture may be multiple, leading to severe kyphosis and a risk of
spinal cord injury.159

Historically, the management of Gaucher disease has been supportive. Given that the disease
is caused by a deficiency in a specific enzyme, modern management involves enzyme
replacement therapy.
Enzyme replacement therapy involves an infusion of a manufactured recombinant DNA
enzyme every 2 weeks and has been shown to substantially reverse the deleterious effects of
the buildup of glucocerebroside.
Patients receiving enzyme replacement therapy feel immediate relief, with less bone pain
and fatigue. The enzyme also enables the reversal of thrombocytopenia and pancytopenia
observed in later stages.
Improvement in the skeletal disease trails behind that of the visceral disease by 2 to 3 years;
however, with continued management, bone mineralization is enhanced, and the risk of
pathologic fracture also can be reduced.161,162
Differential Diagnosis
Several other diseases share some of the findings observed in Gaucher disease; however, the
combination of splenomegaly, thrombocytopenia, and the characteristic bone findings are
relatively unique to Gaucher disease.
Leukemia; lymphoma; various rheumatologic disorders, such as rheumatoid arthritis; and
other lysosomal storage disorders, such as Niemann-Pick disease, also are included in the
differential diagnosis. However, patients with Niemann-Pick disease typically have more liver
involvement than and more extensive neurologic findings than patients with Gaucher
disease.163
The bony manifestations observed in patients with Gaucher disease also can be observed in
patients with various bone metabolic disorders, such as rickets, vitamin C deficiency, copper
deficiency, SCD, and Paget disease; however these disorders typically have other clinical,
laboratory, and radiographic features that differentiate them from Gaucher disease.

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL)/lymphoblastic lymphoma (LBL) is the most common
malignancy found in childhood. Leukemia and lymphoma are malignancies of precursor
T and B cells, or lymphoblasts. The World Health Organization recently recognized these
two malignancies as overlapping presentations of the same disease. If the disease is
found to be primarily nodal and extranodal with less than 20% lymphoblasts in the bone
marrow, it is labeled LBL. If 20% or more lymphoblasts are found in the marrow, a
diagnosis of ALL can be made.164 Pediatric orthopaedic surgeons must keep ALL/LBL in
the differential diagnosis. They often are the first clinicians to evaluate a child because
musculoskeletal pain is a common presenting symptom.165,166
Epidemiology
ALL/LBL comprises 25% of all childhood cancers, with nearly 3,500 cases diagnosed per year in
the United States.
The incidence is 3.5 out of 100,000, with the peak incidence in patients aged 2 to 5 years.
Higher rates are found in males than females.167
Age younger than 1 year and older than 10 years at diagnosis is a poor prognostic indicator.
Survival rates have increased drastically to 80% to 90% since the 1970s.168
Most patients with ALL/LBL have no known genetic or environmental cause; however, certain
genetic conditions such as: neurofibromatosis type 1, Down syndrome, Bloom syndrome, and
ataxia-telangiectasia have been associated with increased risk.169,170
Association with the Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22)(q34;q11) portends an especially poor
prognosis.171
